title: The Ethics and Rationality of Voting

summaries.example: Imagine your class is choosing between two games for Friday. You spend ten minutes learning about the choices and voting. Your vote probably will not decide the result, but you may vote because you want to show support, do your fair share, or help the class choose well. Whether voting is a good choice depends on what you hope your vote will do and what else you could do with those ten minutes.
summaries.summary: Voting can be studied as both a practical choice and a moral action. If someone votes only to change an election’s result, the small chance of being the deciding vote may not seem worth the time and effort. This is sometimes called the paradox of voting. But people may have other goals: they may want to show which ideas or groups they support, enjoy taking part, help create a shared decision, or follow what they believe is a duty. The entry also asks whether citizens should vote in a particular way, whether governments may require voting, whether votes should be bought or sold, and who should have voting rights. These questions have competing answers. For example, compulsory voting might make the voters more like the whole population, but it does not automatically make people more informed or improve every political result. Equal votes may seem fair, while others argue that people with more at stake should have more influence. Systems that give extra power to knowledgeable people might improve decisions, but they could also be biased and unfair.
key_ideas: Voting takes time and effort, so we can ask whether its likely benefits are worth what we give up.
A single vote usually has a very small chance of changing who wins. Some people still vote to express their values, take part, or meet a duty.
People disagree about whether everyone has a moral duty to vote, and whether a person may have a duty to vote carefully and responsibly.
Compulsory voting, selling votes, and deciding who gets to vote raise questions about fairness, freedom, knowledge, and equal treatment.
summaries.why_it_matters: Voting helps decide rules that affect many people, including people who did not vote or who disagree with the result. Thinking carefully about voting can help us separate different questions: What makes voting sensible for one person? What does a citizen owe others? Who belongs in the decision-making group? There is no single answer accepted by everyone, so learning the arguments helps us discuss elections fairly and thoughtfully.

important_terms.definition: A choice is rational when it makes sense for a person’s goal after considering likely benefits, costs, and other choices.
The time, effort, or other benefit you give up when you choose one activity instead of another.
A reason for doing something because the action itself is enjoyable or expresses who you are, not only because it changes an outside result.
A group of people who are considered part of the public that makes a decision together.

questions_to_think_about: If your vote probably will not decide a close contest, what other reasons might you have for voting?
Is it fair to ask everyone to vote, or is doing another helpful civic activity enough?
Should a person vote without learning much about the choices?
Who should count as part of the group making a decision?

summaries.example: Suppose Alex spends an hour researching two candidates. The election is expected to be decided by a wide margin, so Alex’s probability of casting the decisive vote is extremely small. If Alex is considering only the instrumental aim of making the better candidate win, the expected benefit may be lower than the opportunity cost of the hour. But Alex might rationally vote for another reason: to express a political commitment, participate in a collective cause, or fulfill a perceived civic duty. Those reasons change the analysis rather than simply ignoring the low probability of decisiveness.
summaries.summary: The entry examines voting as a problem in both practical rationality and political morality. Under an instrumental model, a voter compares the opportunity cost of voting with the expected value of affecting the result. Because the probability that one vote breaks a tie is generally very small, voting for outcome change may be irrational except in sufficiently close or otherwise unusual circumstances. The analysis becomes different if voters seek a mandate effect, causal participation, expressive satisfaction, or fulfillment of a perceived duty; however, each proposal faces empirical or philosophical challenges. The moral debate then separates a duty to turn out from duties concerning how one votes. The particularity problem challenges arguments that identify a general civic responsibility but do not show why voting is the required way to discharge it. Other views argue that voting can involve complicity, fair contribution, or easy aid, while some claim that ineffective or uninformed voting should be avoided. Further issues concern compulsory voting, vote buying, and the electorate’s membership. Compulsion may reduce demographic inequalities in turnout, but may not improve political competence or substantive representation. Opposition to vote markets appeals variously to equality, efficiency, the common good, secrecy, and the idea that votes are not commodities. Finally, theories of the demos include all affected interests, those subject to coercion, and members of a nation-state; each encounters boundary difficulties. Equal suffrage is defended as egalitarian, while stake-weighted voting and epistocracy challenge it. Epistocracy may address voter incompetence, but can reduce cognitive diversity, produce demographic bias, or lack a justification acceptable to all those—
key_ideas: On an outcome-changing model, the expected value of voting depends on the value difference between candidates, the probability of being decisive, and voting’s opportunity cost. Estimates of decisiveness and candidate effects are disputed.

The mandate hypothesis says a larger electoral victory might give an officeholder greater effectiveness or authority, but empirical work described in the entry challenges the idea that victory margins generally create such a mandate.
Expressive, causal-responsibility, consumption, and duty-based accounts show that voting need not be aimed only at changing who wins.

Arguments for a moral duty to vote include civic virtue, avoiding complicity in injustice, fulfilling a democratic role, and sharing the burden of supporting public goods. The particularity problem asks why voting, rather than another useful civic action, is required.
A right to vote is different from a duty to vote well. Some theories impose epistemic duties: voters should try to form informed, rational judgments because collective decisions affect others.

Compulsory voting might broaden representation because voluntary electorates differ from the population, but the evidence summarized in the entry does not show that compulsion by itself produces better knowledge, representation, or policy outcomes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The ethics of voting matters because electoral decisions exercise power over people who may not share the majority’s views and may not even be allowed to vote. The topic also shows why a simple question such as “Should I vote?” contains several different questions about expected consequences, duties, expression, knowledge, fairness, and political membership. Distinguishing these issues makes it possible to evaluate democracy and its alternatives without assuming that turnout, equal votes, or expertise automatically settles the moral debate.

important_terms.definition: The view that an action is rational when its expected benefits, including benefits to others, exceed its costs and alternatives, given the agent’s goals.
The loss of the best alternative use of time or resources when choosing to vote.
The puzzle that voting can appear irrational because its costs are real while an individual’s chance of changing the result is usually tiny.
A theory that voting can be valuable as a way to express allegiance, identity, values, or political commitments.
The question of who belongs to the political community entitled to participate in collective decisions.
A political system that assigns power partly according to citizens’ knowledge or competence rather than giving everyone the same voting power.
A moral approach that judges some actions wrong because of what they are or what they express, even if their consequences might be good.
A situation in which people who do not contribute still receive benefits produced by others, potentially shifting an unfair burden onto contributors.

questions_to_think_about: If voting has little chance of changing the result, can expressive or duty-based reasons make it rational?
Does a general duty to support good government establish a specific duty to vote, or could other civic actions satisfy it?
Should citizens be permitted to vote on the basis of poorly supported beliefs if the act is legally within their rights?
Would vote markets threaten equality, social meaning, or ballot secrecy even if some transactions produced good outcomes?
Should political power track equal citizenship, personal stakes, or political competence?

summaries.example: A student council election is expected to be a landslide. Maya thinks Candidate A would run events better, but she knows her vote is very unlikely to change the winner. She might still vote because she wants to show support for A, feels that members should do their share, or thinks voting is one way to help the group. Another student might say that Maya should spend the same time checking candidates’ plans or helping organize an event instead. Their disagreement is about both the value of voting and whether voting is special among useful civic actions.
summaries.summary: This entry asks whether voting is rational, morally required, and fairly organized. Voting uses time and effort, so a person who votes only to change an election’s result must compare those costs with the small chance of being decisive and the expected difference between the candidates. This calculation resembles buying a lottery ticket: a very valuable result does not by itself make a low-chance action worthwhile. The conclusion can change if voting has other value. It may express a person’s political identity, show participation in a group, create a sense of causal responsibility, or satisfy a duty to take part. Still, the moral duty to vote is disputed. Some arguments say nonvoters benefit from government without helping provide it; others respond that civic duties can be met through many activities, creating a particularity problem for a vote-specific duty. The entry also distinguishes the right to vote from duties about how to use that right. Compulsory voting is defended as a way to include groups that are underrepresented among voluntary voters, but research discussed in the entry does not show that it automatically improves knowledge or policy. Vote buying is criticized on grounds involving inequality, efficiency, secrecy, and the meaning of voting, though some objections may also apply to persuasion or uninformed voting. Finally, the entry examines who should be in the demos and whether equal suffrage should be replaced by votes weighted by personal stakes or political knowledge.
key_ideas: The answer to whether voting is rational depends on the voter’s aim. Changing the winner is only one possible aim.

A large winning margin may be claimed to give a leader a stronger mandate, but the entry explains that evidence for this effect is weak. Other theories focus on expressing identity or taking causal responsibility.

Supporters of a duty to vote appeal to civic virtue, fairness, avoiding complicity in injustice, and sharing the work of maintaining public goods. Critics ask why voting must be required if volunteering, protesting, or other actions could help too.

A person may have the legal right to vote without having a moral right reason to vote in every possible way. Some philosophers argue that voters should be informed and avoid supporting harmful outcomes.

Compulsory voting could make the electorate more representative, especially if groups that usually vote less are included. Critics note that required turnout does not necessarily create better knowledge or better government.
Debates about equal voting rights include questions about who belongs to the demos and whether equal votes, stake-based votes, or knowledge-based systems are fairest.
summaries.why_it_matters: Elections distribute power, so voting is not only a private preference. It can affect neighbors, minorities, children, nonvoters, and people outside the country making the decision. The arguments help us ask better questions about citizenship: Is fairness about equal participation, equal concern for interests, or competent decisions? Understanding these disagreements supports respectful discussion instead of treating one simple rule as obviously correct.

important_terms.definition: A choice that is sensible when its expected results fit the person’s goal and outweigh the costs of the choice.
What a person gives up by using time or effort for one activity rather than the best available alternative.
The idea that an individual vote usually has a tiny chance of changing an election, even though voting takes effort.
The idea that people may vote to show their identity, loyalties, or values, much as fans show support for a team.
An argument that people who benefit from a shared good should contribute fairly to producing it.
The political group whose members are included in making a decision.
A system that gives political influence partly to people judged more knowledgeable or competent.

questions_to_think_about: Is voting worthwhile when your preferred candidate is almost certain to lose?
Does benefiting from government mean that you owe society a vote? Why might another kind of civic work count instead?
Should being uninformed affect how we judge a person’s vote?
Would compulsory voting make political decisions more representative, or merely increase the number of ballots?
Who should be included when a government’s decision affects people beyond its borders?
